prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony regarding field sobriety exercises (HGN, walk-and-turn, one-leg stand) carries significant weight with Florida juries.
Dashcam and bodycam footage capturing driving pattern and post-stop behavior provides compelling visual evidence.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 20-minute observation period required before breath testing — any belching, regurgitation, or mouth alcohol invalidates the result.
Florida law requires the officer have reasonable suspicion for the initial traffic stop; illegal stops suppress all subsequent evidence.
The Intoxilyzer 8000's maintenance and calibration records are discoverable — gaps or irregularities can exclude breath results.
Rising BAC defense: BAC at time of driving may have been below .08 even if over .08 at time of testing due to absorption curve.
common_defenses: Mouth alcohol contamination — failure to observe 20-minute deprivation period per FDLE breath test procedures.
Rising blood alcohol defense — BAC was below .08 at time of driving but rose above .08 by time of testing.
Medical condition affecting field sobriety — GERD, inner ear issues, neurological conditions, or physical disabilities affected FSE performance.

prosecution_strengths: First-offense DUI in Florida carries mandatory minimum penalties including 50 hours community service or 8 hours imprisonment.
Prosecution can present BAC results as per se evidence of impairment without needing additional proof of driving pattern.
Officers trained in standardized field sobriety testing provide structured testimony under NHTSA protocols.
Florida allows admission of refusal to submit to breath test as evidence of guilt consciousness.
defense_opportunities: First offenders qualify for DUI diversion programs in many Florida counties, potentially avoiding formal conviction.
Contest accuracy of portable breath test (PBT) used at roadside, which is inadmissible at trial but used to establish probable cause.
common_defenses: Breath test machine malfunction — Intoxilyzer 8000 inspection records show maintenance issues, calibration failures, or RFI interference.
Involuntary intoxication — defendant unknowingly consumed alcohol or was drugged by another person.
Independent witness testimony contradicting officer's observations of impairment.

prosecution_strengths: Prior DUI convictions are admissible to establish the enhanced offense and demonstrate pattern of behavior.
Mandatory minimum imprisonment of 10 days (second) or 30 days (third within 10 years) cannot be suspended by the court.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the validity of prior DUI convictions — uncounseled pleas or improper plea colloquies can render priors unusable for enhancement.
File motions to suppress if repeat-offender status was used to justify a more aggressive stop or investigation.
common_defenses: 10-year lookback calculation — prior conviction falls outside the statutory window when calculated from date of prior offense, not conviction.
Constitutional challenge to mandatory minimums as applied — proportionality arguments under the Eighth Amendment.
Suppression of current stop evidence based on Fourth Amendment violations independent of prior record.

prosecution_strengths: Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluations are admissible in Florida and provide structured testimony on drug impairment.
Florida has no per se drug limit, but prosecution need only prove impairment of normal faculties — a lower threshold than BAC-based DUI.
Blood and urine test results showing presence of controlled substances corroborate officer observations of impairment.
defense_opportunities: Unlike alcohol DUI, there is no per se drug impairment level — prosecution must prove actual impairment, not mere presence of substance.
Challenge DRE officer qualifications, training, and the reliability of the 12-step DRE evaluation protocol.
Metabolites of marijuana can remain in the system weeks after use without causing impairment — presence does not equal impairment.
Prescription medication defense — defendant took medication as prescribed by a licensed physician and was not impaired.
common_defenses: Prescription medication taken as directed — valid prescription provides affirmative defense when medication taken within prescribed parameters.
Lack of impairment evidence — mere presence of drug metabolites in blood/urine does not prove impairment at time of driving.
DRE protocol unreliability — the 12-step Drug Recognition Evaluation has been challenged for scientific validity in multiple jurisdictions.
Involuntary intoxication — defendant's drink was spiked or medication interaction was unforeseeable.

prosecution_strengths: Reckless driving requires proving willful or wanton disregard — dashcam footage of speed, weaving, and near-misses is powerful evidence.
Multiple eyewitnesses to dangerous driving corroborate the reckless conduct standard.
Prosecution can present reckless driving as a standalone charge or as a lesser-included of DUI, widening conviction paths.
Accident reconstruction evidence in injury cases can demonstrate speed and deviation from safe driving standards.
defense_opportunities: The willful or wanton disregard standard is higher than ordinary negligence — requires conscious, intentional disregard for safety.
Emergency circumstances (medical emergency, evasion of danger) can negate the willfulness element.
Challenge witness perception — speed estimates by lay witnesses are notoriously unreliable.
Negotiate reckless driving as a plea reduction from DUI, avoiding the DUI-specific collateral consequences.
common_defenses: Emergency doctrine — defendant drove aggressively to avoid a greater harm or respond to a medical emergency.
Mechanical failure — vehicle malfunction (brake failure, tire blowout) caused the dangerous driving pattern.
Misidentification — defendant was not the driver or witness misidentified the vehicle.

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance footage, witness identification, and vehicle damage matching create strong identification evidence.
Consciousness of guilt — fleeing the scene is powerful circumstantial evidence of fault.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether defendant knew or should have known a crash occurred — critical element especially in minor-contact scenarios.
Argue defendant left scene to seek help or due to safety concerns and returned or reported promptly.
Dispute identification evidence — vehicle damage matching is circumstantial and can be challenged.
Knowledge element: prosecution must prove defendant knew the crash resulted in injury/death for enhanced charges.
common_defenses: Duress or safety concerns — defendant left due to threats, dangerous location, or fear for personal safety.
Prompt reporting — defendant left but reported the accident within a reasonable time, mitigating the charge.
Mistaken identity — the vehicle identified was not defendant's or defendant was not driving at the time.

prosecution_strengths: Accident reconstruction evidence establishing speed, point of impact, and deviation from safe driving provides scientific support.
Toxicology reports showing any impairment bolster the recklessness element even though impairment is not a required element.
Victim impact testimony is powerful at sentencing for this Level 7 offense under the Criminal Punishment Code.
Dashcam and surveillance footage near the crash site can graphically demonstrate reckless operation.
defense_opportunities: Challenge accident reconstruction methodology — assumptions about speed, road conditions, and vehicle performance.
Victim's own contributory actions (jaywalking, sudden lane changes) can negate the causation element.
Distinguish from DUI manslaughter — if no impairment, argue the driving behavior did not rise to reckless conduct.
common_defenses: Accident, not recklessness — the driving did not constitute the willful disregard required, distinguishing negligence from recklessness.
Intervening cause — victim's actions, another driver, or road conditions were the superseding cause of death.
Mechanical failure — sudden, unforeseeable vehicle malfunction caused the crash.
Accident reconstruction challenge — prosecution expert's conclusions rest on disputed assumptions about speed, timing, or physics.

prosecution_strengths: Combined proof of DUI impairment plus causation of death creates powerful prosecution case.
Level 8 offense on the Criminal Punishment Code scoresheet — state prison is presumptive.
Permanent driver's license revocation accompanies conviction, demonstrating severity to the jury.
defense_opportunities: Causation is a critical element — argue the death would have occurred regardless of defendant's impairment.
Challenge the BAC or impairment evidence using the same defenses available in underlying DUI cases.
Intervening acts of the victim or third parties may break the chain of causation.
common_defenses: Independent intervening cause — victim's own conduct or a third party's actions were the actual cause of death.
Lack of impairment — challenge BAC results or DRE evaluation to undermine the DUI predicate.
Causation break — even if impaired, the crash was caused by mechanical failure, road conditions, or another driver.
Suppression of DUI evidence — if underlying DUI stop or arrest was unlawful, all derivative evidence is excludable.

prosecution_strengths: Knowledge of suspension is established by DMV records showing notice was mailed — constructive notice is sufficient.
Driving record maintained by DHSMV provides documentary evidence of suspension status.
Officers can verify license status instantly through dispatch or mobile terminals.
defense_opportunities: Challenge actual knowledge of suspension — if defendant never received notice and address on file was wrong.
Verify the suspension was properly imposed — administrative errors in DMV records occur and may invalidate suspension.
First offense without HTO designation is a 2nd degree misdemeanor with minimal penalties — negotiate diversion.
Argue necessity — driving was essential for medical emergency or to avoid imminent harm.
common_defenses: Invalid suspension — the underlying administrative suspension was improperly imposed or had expired.
Necessity defense — defendant drove due to emergency circumstances such as medical emergency or danger to child.
Mistaken identity or driving on wrong person's record — DMV records contain errors.

prosecution_strengths: Dashcam footage from pursuing officer provides real-time evidence of speed, duration, and danger of the flight.
Multiple officers involved in pursuit can corroborate the willful nature of the evasion.
GPS and vehicle speed data from patrol cars establishes exact speeds during pursuit.
Any injuries or property damage during flight can elevate charges to 1st or 2nd degree felony.
defense_opportunities: Florida statute requires officer's emergency lights AND siren be activated — failure to use both creates a valid defense.
Argue defendant did not see or hear the officer due to road conditions, music, or hearing impairment.
Mental health episode or panic attack as explanation for failure to stop, negating willfulness.
common_defenses: Lack of awareness — defendant did not see or hear emergency signals due to loud music, road noise, or hearing impairment.
Fear for safety — defendant reasonably believed the person pursuing was not a legitimate law enforcement officer.
No willful intent — defendant may have been confused about how to safely stop (e.g., no shoulder, unsafe area).

prosecution_strengths: Officer observation of open container in the passenger area during lawful stop is sufficient probable cause.
Open container found incident to DUI arrest corroborates impairment evidence.
Passenger area is broadly defined — includes anywhere reachable from the driver or passenger seat.
defense_opportunities: Defendant was a passenger, not the driver — challenge who possessed the container.
Container was sealed, re-sealed, or contents were not actually alcoholic.
Civil infraction option may be available, avoiding criminal record.
common_defenses: Not an open container — seal was intact, or the container did not actually contain an alcoholic beverage.
Lack of possession — container belonged to another occupant and defendant had no control over it.
Illegal search — officer lacked lawful basis to observe or search the passenger area.

prosecution_strengths: Refusal is admissible at DUI trial as evidence of consciousness of guilt.
Administrative license suspension of 12 months (first) or 18 months (second) is independent of criminal outcome.
Officer's testimony about implied consent warnings and defendant's refusal is straightforward to present.
defense_opportunities: First refusal is a civil/administrative matter only — not a criminal offense itself.
Challenge whether implied consent warnings were properly read before the refusal occurred.
Argue the refusal was not a refusal — defendant was confused, asked questions, or had a language barrier.
Contest the lawfulness of the underlying DUI arrest — implied consent only attaches after lawful arrest.
common_defenses: Unlawful arrest — implied consent is only triggered by a lawful arrest; if the arrest lacked probable cause, refusal is not properly invoked.
Equivocal refusal — defendant's response was ambiguous, asked questions, or requested an attorney rather than flat refusing.
Medical inability — defendant was physically unable to provide a breath sample due to medical condition (COPD, asthma, injury).

prosecution_strengths: Lab analysis confirming the substance as a controlled substance is a strong forensic evidence element.
Constructive possession doctrine allows conviction even when drugs are not found on defendant's person.
Proximity to drug paraphernalia strengthens the possession case.
defense_opportunities: Challenge constructive possession — mere proximity to drugs is insufficient without proof of knowledge and dominion/control.
Motion to suppress based on unlawful search — Fourth Amendment violations in vehicle, home, or person searches.
Challenge lab testing methodology — chain of custody gaps or testing errors can exclude evidence.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the substance was present, especially in shared spaces or borrowed vehicles.
Illegal search and seizure — drugs discovered through warrantless search without valid exception to the warrant requirement.
Temporary possession — defendant briefly held the substance with intent to dispose of it or turn it in.

prosecution_strengths: Field-tested and lab-confirmed cannabis is straightforward to prove at trial.
Over 20 grams automatically becomes a 3rd degree felony, creating significant plea leverage.
Odor of marijuana provides probable cause for vehicle searches under Florida precedent.
Packaging materials and scales found with marijuana support intent-to-distribute upgrades.
defense_opportunities: Many Florida counties have civil citation programs for small amounts (under 20g), diverting from criminal court.
Challenge odor-based probable cause — hemp products are legal and smell identical to marijuana.
Weight challenges — 20-gram felony threshold must include only usable cannabis, not stems, seeds, or packaging.
common_defenses: Illegal search — suppression of evidence obtained without warrant or valid exception, including challenges to odor-based searches.
Weight below felony threshold — total usable cannabis weighed less than 20 grams when properly measured without packaging.
Constructive possession failure — defendant did not have exclusive control over the area where marijuana was found.

prosecution_strengths: Cocaine is Schedule II — any amount constitutes a 3rd degree felony with up to 5 years prison.
Lab confirmation of cocaine hydrochloride or crack cocaine is routine and reliable.
Trafficking thresholds at 28 grams trigger severe mandatory minimums of 3-15 years.
Proximity to cash, scales, and baggies allows upgrade to possession with intent.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the weight — trafficking thresholds include only the weight of the actual cocaine, potentially requiring purity analysis.
Constructive possession requires more than mere proximity — exclusive dominion and control must be proven.
Challenge chain of custody — cocaine evidence must be properly documented from seizure through lab testing.
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — cocaine discovered through unconstitutional search without warrant or valid exception.
Constructive possession failure — cocaine found in common area without evidence tying it specifically to defendant.
Weight dispute — for trafficking charges, challenge whether total weight accurately reflects cocaine content versus cutting agents.
Entrapment — law enforcement induced defendant to purchase or possess cocaine they would not otherwise have possessed.

prosecution_strengths: Methamphetamine trafficking threshold is lower than cocaine (14g vs 28g), triggering mandatory minimums more easily.
Lab testing for methamphetamine is highly reliable and difficult to challenge.
Physical signs of meth use (sores, dental issues, weight loss) can corroborate possession evidence.
Manufacturing evidence (precursors, equipment) often found alongside meth possession strengthens the case.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the weight — the 14-gram trafficking threshold applies to actual methamphetamine, not cutting agents or packaging.
Fourth Amendment suppression motions — meth cases frequently involve questionable stops, searches, and informant tips.
Drug Court eligibility may provide treatment alternative for qualifying defendants.
Challenge field test reliability — field tests have known false-positive rates with certain legal substances.
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — suppression based on unconstitutional traffic stop, home entry, or person search.
Constructive possession challenge — defendant did not have knowledge, dominion, and control over the methamphetamine.
Weight dispute for trafficking — actual meth weight versus total mixture weight including adulterants.
Lack of knowledge — defendant unaware substance was present, particularly in shared living spaces or vehicles.

prosecution_strengths: Fentanyl trafficking threshold is extremely low at 4 grams, easily triggering mandatory minimums.
Lab confirmation readily distinguishes between heroin, fentanyl, and pharmaceutical opioids.
Overdose response evidence (Narcan administration, 911 calls) can establish presence and use.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant actually possessed the substance versus being in proximity to it.
Prescription defense — defendant had a valid prescription for the opioid medication from a licensed practitioner.
Weight challenges — 4-gram fentanyl threshold must reflect actual fentanyl, not total mixture weight.
common_defenses: Valid prescription — defendant possessed opioids pursuant to a valid prescription from a licensed physician.
Constructive possession failure — opioids found in shared space without evidence linking them specifically to defendant.
Illegal search — suppression of evidence obtained through warrantless search or search exceeding scope of warrant.

prosecution_strengths: Possession of someone else's prescription bottle with controlled substances is straightforward to prove.
Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (E-FORCSE) records document prescribing history and identify gaps.
Pharmacy records and practitioner testimony establish whether a valid prescription existed.
Doctor shopping patterns (multiple prescriptions from different practitioners) are well-documented through PDMP.
defense_opportunities: Valid prescription is an affirmative defense — defendant may have had a prescription from a different provider.
Challenge the identification of the substance — loose pills require lab confirmation.
Prescription had not yet been filled, or was recently filled and defendant had leftover medication.
Argue the medication was prescribed but records are incomplete or the prescribing physician's records support the prescription.
common_defenses: Valid prescription defense — defendant had a current, valid prescription for the controlled substance from a licensed practitioner.
Identification failure — loose pills or unmarked containers require laboratory confirmation of the substance.
Illegal search — prescription drugs discovered through unconstitutional search of person, vehicle, or residence.
Pharmacy error — prescription records contain errors or the pharmacist dispensed the wrong medication.

prosecution_strengths: Mandatory minimum sentences cannot be suspended, deferred, or withheld — judges have no discretion below the floor.
Weight-based triggering thresholds are objective — mere possession of threshold quantity equals trafficking regardless of intent.
Federal prosecution threat provides additional leverage in plea negotiations.
Wire evidence (texts, calls, surveillance) often accompanies trafficking investigations.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the weight — prosecution must prove the actual weight of the controlled substance, not total mixture weight for some substances.
Entrapment defense when law enforcement orchestrated the transaction and induced the defendant.
Constructive possession challenges when drugs were found in a shared space or vehicle.
common_defenses: Weight dispute — challenge whether the measured weight accurately reflects the actual controlled substance versus cutting agents, packaging, or moisture.
Illegal search and seizure — trafficking quantities often discovered through wiretaps, informant tips, or searches requiring suppression analysis.
Entrapment — government agents induced the defendant to possess trafficking quantities they would not otherwise have possessed.
Constructive possession — defendant lacked knowledge, dominion, and control over the trafficking quantity.

prosecution_strengths: Controlled buy operations with recorded audio/video provide direct evidence of sale or delivery.
Confidential informant testimony corroborated by surveillance and recorded transactions.
Text messages and phone records documenting drug transactions are admissible and compelling.
defense_opportunities: Challenge informant credibility — informants often have pending cases, cooperation agreements, and bias.
Argue the sale was accommodation (sharing among friends) rather than commercial distribution.
Challenge proximity-enhancement measurements — 1,000-foot distance must be measured correctly from specific points.
Entrapment defense when government agent initiated and encouraged the transaction.
common_defenses: Entrapment — law enforcement induced the sale through persistent requests, and defendant was not predisposed to distribute.
Mere presence — defendant was present during a transaction but was not a participant in the sale or delivery.
Informant reliability — confidential informant is unreliable, has bias, or provided fabricated testimony for their own benefit.
Illegal surveillance — wiretap or electronic monitoring was conducted without proper court authorization under Title III.

prosecution_strengths: Physical evidence of manufacturing operation (precursors, equipment, residue) is compelling.
Expert testimony on manufacturing processes helps jury understand circumstantial evidence.
Environmental contamination evidence from meth labs demonstrates scope and seriousness.
Marijuana grow operations produce photographic evidence of the operation's scale.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether defendant's actions constitute manufacturing versus mere possession of precursors with lawful use.
Manufacturing includes cultivation — but personal-use grows may be argued as simple possession amounts.
Challenge the connection between defendant and the manufacturing operation — mere presence is insufficient.
Illegal entry or search that discovered the operation may be suppressible.
common_defenses: Illegal search — manufacturing operations typically discovered through warrantless entry, overflight, or informant tip requiring warrant analysis.
Lack of participation — defendant was present but did not participate in or have knowledge of the manufacturing operation.
Lawful purpose for precursors — items seized have legitimate household or agricultural uses.
Constructive possession failure — multiple people had access to the manufacturing location.

prosecution_strengths: Residue on paraphernalia provides forensic link between item and controlled substance.
Often charged alongside drug possession, strengthening the overall case.
Intent to use is inferred from proximity to drugs, residue, and defendant statements.
defense_opportunities: Items have lawful alternative uses — pipes for tobacco, scales for cooking or jewelry, baggies for food storage.
Without drug residue, proving the item was intended for drug use requires circumstantial evidence.
Paraphernalia is a 1st degree misdemeanor — potential for diversion, pretrial intervention, or civil citation.
Challenge the search that discovered the paraphernalia.
common_defenses: Lawful use — item has a legitimate non-drug purpose (tobacco pipe, kitchen scale, craft supplies).
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the item was drug paraphernalia or was unaware of drug residue.
Illegal search — paraphernalia discovered through unconstitutional search or seizure.
No connection to controlled substance — item had no residue, no proximity to drugs, and no other indicia of drug use.

prosecution_strengths: Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (E-FORCSE) records provide documentary evidence of doctor shopping patterns.
Pharmacy surveillance footage captures defendant presenting fraudulent prescriptions.
Handwriting analysis and prescription form comparison can establish forgery.
Multiple pharmacy visits in short timeframes establish a pattern of fraud.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether defendant knew the prescription was fraudulent — someone else may have provided it.
Argue defendant had a legitimate medical need and believed the prescription was valid.
Pharmacy and medical records may contain errors that suggest fraud where none existed.
Challenge handwriting analysis methodology and expert qualifications.
common_defenses: Good faith belief — defendant genuinely believed the prescription was valid and had no knowledge of its fraudulent nature.
Medical necessity — defendant had a legitimate medical condition and obtained prescriptions from authorized practitioners.
Identity theft — someone else used defendant's identity to obtain prescriptions fraudulently.
Insufficient evidence of intent to defraud — defendant's actions are consistent with legitimate prescription use.

prosecution_strengths: Circumstantial evidence of intent: quantity, packaging in individual units, scales, cash, and drug ledgers.
Text messages and phone records documenting drug transactions support intent element.
Expert testimony that quantity and packaging are inconsistent with personal use.
Proximity enhancement for areas near schools makes the charge a 1st degree felony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent inference — quantity alone does not prove intent to sell, especially for personal-use addicts.
Absence of typical distribution indicia (scales, baggies, customer lists) undermines intent claim.
Argue all drugs were for personal consumption based on defendant's usage patterns and addiction history.
Challenge the search that discovered the drugs and distribution indicia.
common_defenses: Personal use — defendant possessed the drugs for personal consumption, not distribution, supported by addiction history and usage patterns.
Illegal search and seizure — drugs and indicia of distribution discovered through unconstitutional search.
Constructive possession — defendant did not control the area where drugs and distribution materials were found.
Insufficient evidence of intent — prosecution's circumstantial case fails to exclude reasonable inference of personal use.

prosecution_strengths: Premeditation can be shown by prior threats, planning, procurement of weapon, and manner of killing.
Felony murder doctrine eliminates need to prove premeditation if death occurred during enumerated felony.
DNA evidence, surveillance footage, and digital forensics provide strong identification evidence.
Victim impact evidence is admissible in the penalty phase to support death penalty.
defense_opportunities: Challenge premeditation — argue the killing was spontaneous, in the heat of passion, or without prior reflection.
For felony murder, challenge the underlying felony or argue the death was not a foreseeable consequence.
Challenge forensic evidence — DNA contamination, eyewitness misidentification, false confessions.
common_defenses: Lack of premeditation — the killing was not premeditated, supporting a lesser charge of second-degree murder or manslaughter.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who committed the killing, supported by alibi evidence.
Insanity defense — defendant was unable to understand the nature or consequences of the act due to mental illness (M'Naghten standard in Florida).

prosecution_strengths: Depraved mind standard is lower than premeditation — showing indifference to human life is sufficient.
Often charged as alternative to first-degree murder, giving jury a middle-ground conviction option.
Criminal Punishment Code scoresheet (Level 10) results in significant presumptive prison time.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the depraved mind element — argue conduct was negligent or reckless but not evincing a depraved mind.
Self-defense and Stand Your Ground immunity apply equally to second-degree murder charges.
Downward departure from sentencing guidelines based on mitigating circumstances.
Heat of passion or provocation may reduce the charge to manslaughter.
common_defenses: Self-defense / Stand Your Ground — defendant used force reasonably believing it necessary to prevent death or great bodily harm.
Excusable homicide — death resulted from accident or misfortune without criminal negligence.
Heat of passion — adequate provocation caused defendant to act in sudden passion, reducing to manslaughter.
Lack of depraved mind — defendant's actions, while reckless, did not demonstrate the extreme indifference required.

prosecution_strengths: Manslaughter is often the fallback conviction when murder charges are overcharged — juries may compromise.
Culpable negligence standard, while higher than civil negligence, is easier to prove than depraved mind or premeditation.
Aggravated manslaughter provisions for victims under 18, elderly, or disabled carry 30-year maximums.
Firearm enhancements under 10-20-Life still apply to manslaughter convictions.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense claim — even if found not fully justified, may reduce from murder to manslaughter.
Provocation defense — adequate provocation by the victim caused defendant to act in sudden heat of passion.
Challenge causation — argue the death resulted from intervening causes rather than defendant's actions.
Excusable homicide — death was an accident or misfortune with no criminal intent or negligence.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant acted in reasonable belief of imminent danger, even if the force used was found to be excessive.
Provocation/heat of passion — adequate provocation caused defendant to act in sudden passion before a reasonable cooling period.

prosecution_strengths: Culpable negligence encompasses a wide range of reckless behavior resulting in death.
Expert testimony on standard of care demonstrates how defendant's conduct was grossly negligent.
Medical examiner testimony establishing cause and manner of death links defendant's conduct to the victim's death.
defense_opportunities: Argue conduct was ordinary negligence, not the gross and flagrant culpable negligence required.
Challenge causation — the death resulted from pre-existing conditions or intervening events.
Accident defense — death was truly accidental with no reckless disregard for human life.
Expert witnesses can testify that defendant's conduct was within the range of reasonable behavior.
common_defenses: Ordinary negligence — defendant's conduct was careless but did not rise to the gross and flagrant standard of culpable negligence.
Intervening cause — victim's own actions or a third party's actions were the proximate cause of death.
Accident — death was the result of a genuine accident without criminal negligence.
Lack of foreseeability — a reasonable person would not have foreseen that the conduct could result in death.

prosecution_strengths: 10-20-Life mandatory minimums apply when a firearm is used — 3-year minimum for carrying, 20 years for discharge.
Victim testimony about fear and the weapon creates powerful emotional evidence for the jury.
No physical contact required for conviction — threat plus ability plus fear is sufficient.
Enhanced penalties for victims who are law enforcement, children under 12, or elderly.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the deadly weapon element — argue the object used does not qualify as a deadly weapon under Florida law.
Self-defense/Stand Your Ground — defendant had a reasonable fear of imminent harm and responded defensively.
No well-founded fear — victim's claimed fear was not reasonable under the circumstances.
Conditional threat defense — a mere conditional or future threat does not create imminent fear.
common_defenses: Not a deadly weapon — the object used or displayed does not meet the legal definition of a deadly weapon.
No intent — defendant did not intend to threaten the victim; the action was misinterpreted.
Lack of imminence — the alleged threat was conditional or referred to future action, not imminent violence.

prosecution_strengths: Low threshold for conviction — intentional threat plus ability plus fear of imminent violence.
Victim and witness testimony about the threatening behavior is often sufficient.
No physical contact needed — purely verbal threats with apparent ability to carry out suffice.
Often charged alongside other offenses, creating cumulative case pressure.
defense_opportunities: Words alone without an overt act do not constitute assault — there must be an accompanying act.
Challenge whether the victim's fear was reasonable and well-founded under the circumstances.
Self-defense — defendant's threatening conduct was in response to the victim's prior aggression.
As a 2nd degree misdemeanor, simple assault is eligible for pretrial diversion in most counties.
common_defenses: Words alone — mere verbal threats without accompanying physical act do not constitute assault under Florida law.
No reasonable fear — the alleged victim had no well-founded fear of imminent violence under the circumstances.
Self-defense — defendant acted in reasonable response to victim's aggression or threats.
Mutual combat — both parties were equally engaged in threatening behavior.

prosecution_strengths: Any unwanted touching satisfies the element — even slight contact qualifies if against the victim's will.
Medical records documenting injuries corroborate the battery allegation.
Victim testimony about the unwanted contact is often the primary and sufficient evidence.
defense_opportunities: Consent — the physical contact was consensual (mutual combat, sports, horseplay).
Self-defense — defendant was responding to the victim's initial aggression.
Accidental contact — the touching was not intentional.
As a 1st degree misdemeanor, diversion programs and alternative sentencing are available.
common_defenses: Consent — alleged victim consented to the physical contact (mutual combat, consensual activity).
Accidental contact — the touching was unintentional and not willful or knowing.
Mutual combat — both parties voluntarily engaged in physical altercation.

prosecution_strengths: Medical evidence of great bodily harm, permanent disability, or disfigurement is powerful.
10-20-Life mandatory minimums apply when firearms are used — 10-year minimum for possession during the offense.
Enhanced to 1st degree felony when victim is law enforcement, elderly, pregnant, or disabled.
Photographs of injuries create lasting impression on jurors.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the great bodily harm element — injuries may not rise to permanent disability or disfigurement.
Self-defense with Stand Your Ground immunity — defendant reasonably feared great bodily harm.
Deadly weapon challenge — argue the object used does not qualify as a deadly weapon.
Injury was accidental during a mutual altercation — lack of specific intent to cause great bodily harm.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant used force reasonably believed necessary to prevent imminent great bodily harm or death.
Injuries not great bodily harm — victim's injuries do not meet the legal threshold of great bodily harm, permanent disability, or disfigurement.
Lack of intent — defendant did not intentionally or knowingly cause great bodily harm; the injury was an unintended consequence.
Defense of others — defendant acted to protect a third party from imminent unlawful force.

prosecution_strengths: Victim identification testimony is powerful even without physical evidence.
Surveillance footage from businesses provides visual evidence of the robbery.
10-20-Life firearm enhancements create severe mandatory minimums if any weapon was used.
Fear element is broadly interpreted — implied threats satisfy the force requirement.
defense_opportunities: Challenge victim identification — cross-racial identification, stress, lighting conditions affect reliability.
Argue the taking lacked force or fear — may reduce to theft charge.
Afterthought doctrine — if force was used after the taking was complete, it may not constitute robbery.
Alibi defense — defendant was not present at the location of the robbery.
common_defenses: Mistaken identification — victim misidentified defendant due to stress, poor lighting, or cross-racial identification issues.
No force or fear — the taking occurred without force, violence, or putting in fear, reducing the offense to theft.
Alibi — defendant was not at the location of the robbery and can prove their whereabouts.
Claim of right — defendant genuinely believed the property belonged to them (negates intent to deprive).

prosecution_strengths: Life felony with 10-year mandatory minimum under 10-20-Life — extremely strong plea leverage.
Weapon does not need to be loaded or functional — appearance of a weapon suffices.
If firearm discharged, 20-year mandatory minimum; if injury or death, 25-year minimum.
Surveillance footage, victim testimony, and weapon recovery create overwhelming evidence packages.
defense_opportunities: Challenge weapon identification — argue the object was not actually a firearm or deadly weapon.
Mistaken identification — same challenges as robbery plus weapon-focus effect reducing identification accuracy.
Withdrawal — defendant voluntarily abandoned the robbery before completion.
Challenge 10-20-Life application — argue the weapon was not actually carried during the commission of the offense.
common_defenses: Misidentification — weapon-focus effect causes witnesses to focus on the weapon rather than the perpetrator's face.
Not a deadly weapon — the alleged weapon was a toy, replica, or did not meet the legal definition.
Duress — defendant committed the robbery under threat of imminent death or serious bodily harm from a third party.
Alibi — defendant was not present and was misidentified through unreliable witness testimony or lineup procedures.

prosecution_strengths: Life felony carrying potential life imprisonment — enormous plea leverage.
Victim testimony about confinement, movement, and fear is compelling.
Intent element (ransom, shield, commit felony, inflict harm, terrorize) is broadly interpreted.
When combined with sexual battery on a child, mandatory life sentence with no possibility of parole.
defense_opportunities: Fahy/Mobley merger doctrine — movement incidental to another felony may not support separate kidnapping charge.
Challenge the confinement element — brief or minor restriction may not constitute kidnapping.
Consent — alleged victim voluntarily accompanied defendant.
common_defenses: Consent — alleged victim accompanied defendant voluntarily and was not confined against their will.
No felony intent — defendant's purpose was not among the enumerated intents (ransom, commission of felony, etc.).
Parental rights — in custodial disputes, parent's movement of child may be defended under parental authority.

prosecution_strengths: Fire investigation evidence (accelerant detection, point of origin, burn patterns) provides scientific proof.
Surveillance footage capturing defendant near the fire scene before ignition.
Insurance fraud motive provides clear evidence of intent when structure was insured.
1st degree felony for occupied structures or any dwelling carries up to 30 years.
defense_opportunities: Challenge fire investigation methodology — NFPA 921 standards require ruling out accidental causes first.
Accidental fire — electrical malfunction, cooking accident, or other non-criminal cause.
Challenge defendant's connection to the fire — proximity or ownership alone is insufficient.
Mens rea challenge — defendant did not willfully or intentionally start the fire.
common_defenses: Accidental origin — fire was caused by electrical malfunction, equipment failure, or natural causes, not intentional act.
Faulty fire investigation — investigators failed to follow NFPA 921 methodology or reached conclusions unsupported by evidence.
Lack of intent — defendant did not willfully cause the fire; it was an accident or unintended consequence.
Alibi — defendant was not present at the location when the fire was started.

prosecution_strengths: Overt act toward commission (shooting, stabbing, poisoning) provides direct evidence of intent.
Victim survival and testimony about the attack is compelling.
10-20-Life firearm enhancements apply — 10 years for carrying, 20 for discharge, 25 for injury.
Prior threats, planning evidence, and weapon procurement establish premeditated intent.
defense_opportunities: Challenge premeditation — argue the act was spontaneous, reducing to attempted second-degree murder.
Self-defense — defendant was responding to victim's aggression or threat.
Voluntary abandonment — defendant voluntarily stopped the attempt before completion.
Challenge intent to kill — actions may demonstrate intent to injure but not to kill.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant reasonably believed deadly force was necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm.
Lack of intent to kill — defendant intended to injure or frighten, not to kill the victim.
No premeditation — for attempted first-degree murder, the act was spontaneous, not premeditated.

prosecution_strengths: Same as aggravated assault — weapon display plus threat plus reasonable fear.
10-20-Life mandatory minimum of 3 years when firearm is carried during the offense.
Victim testimony about the weapon and resulting fear is powerful.
Medical evidence of any injuries corroborates the assault.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the object constitutes a deadly weapon under Florida law.
Self-defense — defendant displayed weapon defensively in response to victim's aggression.
Stand Your Ground immunity hearing — if successful, charges are dismissed entirely.
No intent to threaten — defendant's display of the weapon was not intended as a threat.
common_defenses: Self-defense / Stand Your Ground — defendant displayed weapon in reasonable response to imminent threat.
Object is not a deadly weapon — the item does not meet the legal definition of a weapon likely to produce death or great bodily harm.
No intent — defendant did not intend to threaten; weapon display was accidental or for lawful purpose.
No imminent fear — alleged victim had no reasonable, well-founded fear of imminent violence.

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance footage from businesses and parking lots captures the taking.
Confession or admission during loss prevention encounter.
Recovery of stolen property on defendant's person or in their vehicle.
Value of property determines the charge level — over $750 is a felony in Florida.
defense_opportunities: Challenge intent to permanently deprive — borrowing or mistake negates the intent element.
Value dispute — if property value is under $750, the offense is only petit theft (2nd degree misdemeanor).
Claim of right — defendant genuinely believed the property was theirs.
Pretrial diversion available for first-time theft offenders in most Florida counties.
common_defenses: Lack of intent — defendant did not intend to permanently deprive the owner of the property.
Claim of right — defendant had a good faith belief that the property belonged to them.
Value dispute — the property was worth less than $750, making it a misdemeanor rather than a felony.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who committed the theft.

prosecution_strengths: Documentation of property value through receipts, appraisals, and owner testimony.
Surveillance evidence, witness testimony, and recovered property build a strong case.
Higher theft amounts trigger more serious felony degrees (3rd: $750-$20K; 2nd: $20K-$100K; 1st: $100K+).
defense_opportunities: Challenge the valuation of property — market value may be lower than claimed, reducing the charge degree.
Argue the taking was temporary (unauthorized borrowing) without intent to permanently deprive.
Challenge the chain of evidence showing the property was in defendant's possession.
Claim of right defense when defendant believed they had ownership or right to the property.
common_defenses: Value below threshold — property's fair market value is below $750, reducing charge to petit theft.
Lack of intent to permanently deprive — defendant intended to return the property (borrowing defense).
Claim of right — defendant had a good faith belief in their right to possess the property.
Consent — property owner authorized the defendant to take or use the property.

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance footage from retail establishments provides clear evidence of the taking.
Loss prevention officer testimony about observing the concealment and failure to pay.
Recovery of merchandise on defendant provides direct evidence.
defense_opportunities: First-time offender diversion programs available in most Florida counties.
Challenge the intent element — defendant may have been distracted, confused, or intended to pay.
Value challenge — ensure the property is valued at fair market value, not retail price.
As a 2nd degree misdemeanor (first offense), penalties are minimal.
common_defenses: Lack of intent — defendant absent-mindedly left the store without paying, was distracted, or intended to pay.
Diversion/pretrial intervention — first-time offenders qualify for programs that result in dismissal upon completion.
Value dispute — property value was overstated by the merchant.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who took the property.

prosecution_strengths: Loss prevention video, witness testimony, and recovery of merchandise provide comprehensive evidence.
Anti-shoplifting civil demand adds financial consequences beyond criminal penalties.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the detention by store personnel — must be reasonable in manner, scope, and duration.
First-offense diversion programs widely available in Florida.
Factual innocence — defendant had a receipt, had already paid, or merchandise was their own property.
common_defenses: No intent to steal — defendant intended to pay, was comparison shopping, or forgot item was in their possession.
Improper merchant detention — store personnel exceeded reasonable bounds in detaining defendant.
Already purchased — defendant had a receipt or proof of prior purchase for the item.
Diversion eligibility — first-time offenders qualify for pretrial intervention programs.

prosecution_strengths: Physical evidence of entry (tool marks, broken locks, damaged windows) demonstrates the unlawful entry.
Surveillance footage, forensic evidence (fingerprints, DNA), and witness testimony establish identity.
Burglary of a dwelling is a 2nd degree felony; with assault or dangerous weapon becomes 1st degree life felony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent element — defendant entered without intent to commit an offense (intent formed after entry).
Consent to enter — defendant had permission or authorization to be in the structure.
Remaining after being asked to leave, without forming criminal intent, may not constitute burglary.
common_defenses: Consent/authorization — defendant had permission to enter or remain in the structure and did not intend to commit an offense.
No intent at time of entry — defendant's intent to commit an offense formed after lawful entry, negating the burglary element.
Mistaken identity — forensic evidence does not conclusively link defendant to the scene.
Structure does not qualify — the location does not meet the statutory definition of a dwelling, structure, or conveyance.

prosecution_strengths: Becomes a 1st degree life felony if defendant armed, commits assault, or uses a vehicle to damage the dwelling.
Victims' testimony about invasion of their home carries enormous emotional weight.
DNA, fingerprints, and digital evidence (cell phone location) provide strong forensic identification.
defense_opportunities: Consent defense — defendant was invited or had a right to be in the dwelling.
Challenge forensic evidence linking defendant to the scene — contamination, chain of custody, or alternate explanations.
Abandonment — defendant voluntarily left before completing the intended offense.
common_defenses: Authorization to enter — defendant had an invitation, key, or right to access the dwelling.
Not a dwelling — structure does not meet statutory definition of dwelling or curtilage.
Insufficient forensic evidence — prints, DNA, or other evidence does not conclusively identify defendant.
No intent to commit offense inside — defendant entered for a lawful purpose (to retrieve personal property, seek shelter).

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance systems in commercial structures provide direct evidence of entry and conduct.
Alarm system records document precise time of unauthorized entry.
Tools and equipment used for entry recovered from defendant link them to the offense.
Serial burglary patterns allow prosecution to introduce similar-act evidence.
defense_opportunities: Business was open or defendant believed it was open to the public at the time of entry.
Defendant entered without intent to commit an offense — intent formed after entry.
Challenge surveillance quality — grainy or unclear footage may not provide reliable identification.
Reduce to trespass if prosecution cannot prove intent to commit an offense inside.
common_defenses: Open to public — defendant entered during business hours or believed the business was open.
No criminal intent — defendant entered for a lawful purpose and did not intend to commit an offense.
Mistaken identity — surveillance footage is unclear or witness identification is unreliable.
Trespass, not burglary — defendant entered without permission but without intent to commit an additional offense.

prosecution_strengths: Vehicle identification through VIN, registration, and GPS tracking provides strong identification evidence.
LoJack and GPS systems allow real-time tracking and recovery linking defendant to the stolen vehicle.
Owner testimony that they did not give permission is straightforward to establish.
defense_opportunities: Claim of right or authorization — defendant believed they had permission to use the vehicle.
Joyriding/temporary use — defendant intended to return the vehicle, negating intent to permanently deprive.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who took the vehicle.
Challenge the unauthorized nature of the taking — keys were left in the vehicle or given to defendant.
common_defenses: Authorization — defendant had permission or a good-faith belief in permission to use the vehicle.
Temporary use — defendant intended to return the vehicle and did not intend to permanently deprive the owner (joyriding defense).
Claim of right — defendant believed they had an ownership interest in the vehicle (co-owner, secured party).
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who initially took the vehicle.

prosecution_strengths: Possession of recently stolen property creates a rebuttable presumption of knowledge under Florida case law.
Serial numbers, registration, and ownership records confirm the property was stolen.
Undercover operations and surveillance document defendant receiving known stolen goods.
Low purchase price relative to value suggests knowledge of stolen nature.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the knowledge element — defendant did not know or have reason to know the property was stolen.
Legitimate purchase from an apparently lawful source — receipt or documentation of transaction.
Claim of right — defendant believed they had a right to the property.
Challenge the chain of evidence showing the property was actually stolen.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the property was stolen and had no reason to suspect it.
Good faith purchase — defendant bought the property for fair value from an apparently legitimate source.
Property was not actually stolen — the property was abandoned, discarded, or given away by the owner.
Innocent possession — defendant came into possession innocently and reported or attempted to return the property.

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance footage and witness testimony identify the person causing damage.
Damage estimates from repair professionals document the extent and cost of destruction.
defense_opportunities: Challenge damage valuation — lower value may reduce from felony to misdemeanor.
Accidental damage — conduct was not willful and malicious.
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who caused the damage.
Consent — property owner authorized or consented to the modification.
common_defenses: Value dispute — repair costs are inflated, reducing the charge level below felony threshold.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who damaged the property.
Consent or authorization — property owner permitted the defendant to alter the property.

prosecution_strengths: Notice to leave (verbal warning, trespass warning, posted signs) establishes the unlawful-remaining element.
Prior trespass warnings documented by law enforcement create a clear record.
Business owner or property manager testimony about lack of authorization.
Trespass in a structure or conveyance is a 2nd degree misdemeanor; trespass on property is a 1st degree misdemeanor.
defense_opportunities: Lack of notice — defendant did not receive adequate notice that they were not authorized to be present.
Authorization or invitation — defendant had a reasonable belief they were permitted to be on the property.
Necessity — defendant entered the property due to emergency circumstances.
First Amendment expression — on public property or quasi-public spaces, free speech may apply.
common_defenses: No notice — defendant was not warned to leave or did not see posted signage prohibiting entry.
Invitation or authorization — defendant had permission from an authorized person to be on the property.
Necessity — defendant trespassed due to emergency (seeking shelter from storm, fleeing danger).
Public access — the property was open to the public and defendant's presence was lawful.

prosecution_strengths: Property damage evidence (photos, repair estimates, video) directly demonstrates the offense.
Value-based charging tiers: under $200 (2nd degree misd.), $200-$1,000 (1st degree misd.), over $1,000 (3rd degree felony).
Witness identification and surveillance footage link defendant to the damage.
Restitution for the full cost of repair is mandatory upon conviction.
defense_opportunities: Accidental damage — defendant did not act willfully and maliciously.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who caused the damage.
Negotiate restitution agreement for charge reduction or diversion.
common_defenses: Accidental damage — the damage was not willful and malicious; it was an accident.
Value below threshold — damage cost is below $1,000, making it a misdemeanor rather than felony.
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who caused the property damage.
Consent — property owner authorized the conduct that resulted in the damage.

prosecution_strengths: Excited utterance and 911 call recordings are admissible even if victim later recants.
No-drop prosecution policy in many Florida State Attorney offices — cases proceed even without victim cooperation.
Bodycam footage capturing victim statements, injuries, and scene conditions.
defense_opportunities: Victim recantation — while prosecution can proceed, lack of victim cooperation weakens the case.
Self-defense — defendant was the actual victim responding to the other party's aggression.
Mutual combat — both parties engaged in violence; primary aggressor determination may be challenged.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant was defending against the other party's aggression and was not the primary aggressor.
False accusation — victim fabricated the allegation for leverage in a custody, divorce, or other family matter.
Insufficient evidence — prosecution cannot prove the case beyond reasonable doubt without victim testimony.

prosecution_strengths: Photographs of injuries taken at the scene provide compelling evidence.
911 recordings and excited utterances admissible under hearsay exception regardless of victim cooperation.
Mandatory 29-point batterers' intervention program and 12-month probation upon conviction.
defense_opportunities: Primary aggressor challenge — argue the other party was the initial aggressor.
Self-defense — defendant reacted to protect themselves from the other party's unlawful force.
Minor or no injuries inconsistent with the alleged battery.
Challenge the credibility of the complainant — motive to fabricate in custody or divorce context.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant used reasonable force to protect themselves from the other party's violence.
False accusation — allegation fabricated for strategic advantage in family court proceedings.
Accidental contact — the touching was not intentional during an argument or while gesturing.
Primary aggressor misidentification — responding officer incorrectly identified the primary aggressor.

prosecution_strengths: DCF (Department of Children and Families) investigation records provide professional assessment of risk.
Medical evidence of child's condition supports prosecution's narrative of endangerment.
Mandatory reporter testimony from teachers, doctors, or counselors.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the definition of endangerment — the conduct did not create a substantial risk of harm.
Parenting disagreement — conduct was within the range of legitimate parenting choices.
Lack of knowledge — defendant was unaware of the dangerous condition affecting the child.
Cultural or religious practices may provide context for parenting decisions.
common_defenses: No substantial risk — the child was not placed in a situation that endangered their physical or mental health.
Reasonable parenting — defendant's actions were within the range of acceptable parenting decisions.
Lack of willful or culpable negligence — defendant's conduct was not grossly negligent.
Third-party responsibility — another caregiver created the dangerous condition without defendant's knowledge.

prosecution_strengths: Medical evidence including X-rays, CT scans, and expert testimony on pattern injuries.
Child Protective Team (CPT) forensic interviews provide trained assessments.
Prior DCF history and documented concerns establish a pattern.
defense_opportunities: Challenge medical testimony — injuries may have alternative explanations (accidental, medical condition).
Accidental injury — child's injury resulted from normal childhood activity, not abuse.
Misidentification of abuser — another caregiver or person inflicted the injury.
Reasonable discipline defense — Florida permits reasonable corporal punishment that does not result in significant injury.
common_defenses: Accidental injury — the child's injury resulted from a fall, play, or other non-abusive cause.
Alternative perpetrator — another person with access to the child caused the injury.
Medical condition — the child has a condition (brittle bone disease, easy bruising disorder) that explains the injuries.

prosecution_strengths: Injunction/protective order is a court document — violation is straightforward to prove.
Contact evidence through phone records, texts, emails, social media, and GPS data.
Victim testimony about the contact or approach violating the order.
Florida treats violation of injunction as a 1st degree misdemeanor or 3rd degree felony (if with violence).
defense_opportunities: Challenge knowledge of the order — defendant was not properly served or did not know the order's terms.
Accidental or incidental contact — defendant encountered the protected person unintentionally.
Victim initiated the contact — the protected person contacted the defendant first.
The order was improperly issued or has expired.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant was not properly served with the order and did not know its terms.
Unintentional contact — the encounter was accidental and not a willful violation of the order.
Victim-initiated contact — the protected person voluntarily initiated the contact.
Invalid order — the injunction was improperly issued, lacked jurisdiction, or had expired.

prosecution_strengths: Pattern of conduct documented through texts, emails, social media, surveillance, and GPS tracking.
Victim testimony about emotional distress and fear for safety.
Aggravated stalking (with threats) is a 3rd degree felony carrying up to 5 years.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the pattern element — isolated incidents do not constitute a course of conduct.
First Amendment — conduct involves protected speech or expression, not threats.
No reasonable fear — the alleged victim's fear was not objectively reasonable.
Legitimate purpose for the contact — work-related, shared custody, or other lawful reason.
common_defenses: No course of conduct — the behavior was isolated, not a repeated pattern of harassment.
Legitimate purpose — contact was for a lawful reason (shared children, business, debt collection).
No credible threat — statements or conduct did not rise to a level creating reasonable fear.
First Amendment protected activity — conduct involved protected speech, protest, or expression.

prosecution_strengths: Medical evidence of neglect or abuse in elderly victims is often severe and well-documented.
Mandatory reporting by healthcare workers ensures institutional awareness and documentation.
Aggravated abuse of an elderly person is a 1st degree felony carrying up to 30 years.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the victim meets the statutory definition of elderly or disabled.
Accident — injuries resulted from falls or other accidents common among the elderly.
Caregiver resource limitations — lack of resources rather than willful neglect.
Medical condition — victim's condition deteriorated due to their underlying health issues, not defendant's actions.
common_defenses: Accidental injury — elderly victims are prone to falls and injuries unrelated to abuse.
No willful act — defendant did not intentionally or knowingly cause harm or neglect the victim.
Caregiver limitations — defendant lacked the training, resources, or awareness to provide adequate care.
Medical causation — victim's condition resulted from pre-existing medical conditions, not defendant's conduct.

prosecution_strengths: Physical recovery of the weapon with forensic evidence (fingerprints, DNA) linking it to defendant.
Open carry prohibition provides straightforward enforcement for visible weapons.
defense_opportunities: Second Amendment challenges — ongoing litigation about the scope of constitutional carry rights.
Challenge constructive possession — weapon found in shared space without proof of defendant's knowledge and control.
common_defenses: Constitutional challenge — Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms as applied to defendant's circumstances.
Constructive possession failure — weapon found in common area without proof of defendant's knowledge and control.
Temporary/innocent possession — defendant briefly handled the weapon for a lawful purpose (self-defense, securing it).

prosecution_strengths: Prior felony conviction is easily proven through court records and FDLE criminal history.
Physical recovery of the firearm in defendant's possession or accessible location.
10-20-Life mandatory minimum of 3 years applies to felon in actual possession of a firearm.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether defendant actually or constructively possessed the firearm.
Prior felony conviction may have been restored — civil rights restoration can negate the felony predicate.
The prior conviction was an out-of-state offense that may not qualify as a felony under Florida law.
Temporary or innocent possession — defendant possessed firearm briefly to prevent harm or secure it.
common_defenses: No possession — defendant did not actually or constructively possess the firearm found nearby.
Rights restored — defendant's civil rights, including firearm rights, were restored after the prior felony conviction.
Prior conviction does not qualify — the predicate offense is not a felony under Florida law or has been expunged.
Temporary/justifiable possession — defendant possessed the firearm momentarily for self-defense or to prevent harm.

prosecution_strengths: Ballistic evidence, shell casings, and bullet trajectories reconstruct the shooting.
Witness testimony about hearing gunshots and seeing the defendant.
ShotSpotter or similar gunshot detection systems provide time and location data.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense — defendant discharged the firearm to protect against imminent threat.
Accidental discharge — weapon discharged unintentionally.
Challenge identification — defendant was not the person who fired the weapon.
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant fired in reasonable defense against imminent threat of death or great bodily harm.
Accidental discharge — the firearm discharged unintentionally due to mechanical malfunction or accident.
Not in public — the discharge occurred on private property in a lawful manner.
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who discharged the firearm.

prosecution_strengths: Physical evidence of the prohibited weapon with forensic testing confirming its characteristics.
Expert testimony classifying the weapon as prohibited under Florida law.
Possession alone, without use, is sufficient for conviction.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the classification — weapon may not actually meet the statutory definition of a prohibited weapon.
Lawful possession exception — antique firearms, curios, or relics may be exempt.
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the weapon's characteristics made it prohibited.
Fourth Amendment challenge — weapon discovered through illegal search.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the weapon was prohibited or modified to prohibited specifications.
Illegal search — weapon discovered through warrantless search without valid exception.
Antique or curio exemption — weapon qualifies for an exemption from the prohibited weapons statute.

prosecution_strengths: Electronic communications (emails, texts, wire transfers) provide documented evidence of the scheme.
Financial records trace the movement of funds through the fraudulent scheme.
Victim testimony about reliance on fraudulent representations.
Pattern evidence showing multiple victims strengthens the scheme element.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent to defraud — defendant genuinely believed in the legitimacy of the transaction.
No use of interstate wires — the fraudulent scheme did not involve wire communications.
Good faith defense — defendant acted in good faith without intent to deceive.
Statute of limitations — wire fraud has a 5-year federal statute of limitations.
common_defenses: Good faith — defendant genuinely believed the representations were true and had no intent to defraud.
No scheme to defraud — the transaction was legitimate and not part of a fraudulent scheme.
No material misrepresentation — the alleged false statement was not material to the victim's decision.
Statute of limitations — the prosecution was filed beyond the applicable limitations period.

prosecution_strengths: Digital evidence including IP addresses, device fingerprints, and login records trace the fraud to defendant.
Financial records showing fraudulent transactions in victim's name.
Victim testimony about unauthorized use of their personal information.
defense_opportunities: Authorization — defendant had permission to use the identification information.
Mistaken identity — defendant's own identity or device was stolen/misused by the actual perpetrator.
No fraudulent intent — use of information was for a lawful purpose.
Challenge digital evidence — IP addresses and device information can be spoofed.
common_defenses: Authorization — victim gave defendant permission to use their personal information.
Defendant was also a victim — defendant's own identity was compromised and used without their knowledge.
No fraudulent purpose — defendant used the information without intent to defraud or obtain anything of value.
Insufficient digital evidence — IP addresses, devices, and accounts can be compromised by third parties.

prosecution_strengths: Financial records, audit trails, and accounting evidence document the misappropriation.
Bank records and electronic transaction records trace the diversion of funds.
Expert forensic accounting testimony presenting complex financial evidence to the jury.
defense_opportunities: Authorization — defendant had permission or good faith belief in permission to use the funds.
Claim of right — defendant believed they were owed the money (bonus, commission, reimbursement).
Accounting errors — apparent discrepancies result from bookkeeping mistakes, not theft.
Intent challenge — defendant intended to repay the funds and did not intend to permanently deprive.
common_defenses: Authorization — defendant believed they had permission to make the transfers or expenditures.
Claim of right — defendant believed they were owed the funds as compensation, bonus, or reimbursement.
Accounting error — the apparent misappropriation is explained by bookkeeping mistakes or accounting irregularities.
Lack of intent — defendant intended to repay the funds and did not intend to permanently deprive the employer.

prosecution_strengths: Handwriting analysis comparing questioned documents to known defendant samples.
Document examination revealing alterations, inconsistencies, or fabrication techniques.
Digital forensics can trace document creation and alteration on defendant's devices.
defense_opportunities: Authorization — defendant had permission from the document owner to sign or alter the document.
No intent to defraud — defendant signed or altered the document without fraudulent purpose.
Challenge handwriting analysis — forensic handwriting comparison has known reliability limitations.
Mistake or misunderstanding — defendant did not realize the document was not authentic.
common_defenses: Authorization — defendant had permission to sign or was acting as an authorized agent.
No intent to defraud or injure — defendant's purpose was not to deceive or obtain something of value.
Not a legally operative document — the forged document does not meet the statutory definition of a forgeable instrument.
Challenge handwriting analysis — expert's methodology and conclusions can be disputed.

prosecution_strengths: Bank records documenting insufficient funds or closed account at time of presentment.
Pattern of writing bad checks across multiple merchants.
defense_opportunities: Account had sufficient funds at the time of writing — insufficient funds arose later.
Post-dated checks are not covered by the worthless check statute.
Challenge the demand letter — proper service requirements must be met.
common_defenses: Good faith — defendant believed the account had sufficient funds at the time the check was written.
Post-dated check — the check was post-dated with the payee's knowledge, excluding it from the statute.

prosecution_strengths: Investigation records from insurance company special investigation units (SIU).
Surveillance footage contradicting claimed injuries or losses.
Expert testimony from claims adjusters and fraud investigators.
defense_opportunities: Good faith claim — defendant genuinely believed the claim was valid and accurate.
Dispute over claim value — disagreement about the extent of loss is not fraud.
Insurance company denial is not evidence of fraud — disagreements about coverage are civil matters.
Challenge surveillance evidence — context and timing may be misleading.
common_defenses: Good faith belief — defendant honestly believed the information in the claim was accurate.
No material misrepresentation — the alleged false statement was an honest mistake or estimate.
Claim dispute — disagreement about claim value is a civil matter, not criminal fraud.
Insurance company bad faith — the insurer has a motive to deny legitimate claims.

prosecution_strengths: Transaction records with timestamps and locations link defendant to fraudulent purchases.
Surveillance footage at point of sale showing defendant using the card.
Digital evidence on defendant's devices showing stolen card numbers or fraud tools.
defense_opportunities: Authorization — cardholder gave defendant permission to use the card.
Mistaken identity — defendant's identity was stolen and used by the actual perpetrator.
Challenge the identification linking defendant to the fraudulent transactions.
No knowledge — defendant did not know the card was unauthorized or stolen.
common_defenses: Authorization — defendant had the cardholder's permission to use the credit card.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who made the fraudulent transactions.
No knowledge — defendant did not know the card was stolen, unauthorized, or that the transactions were fraudulent.
Cardholder acquiescence — cardholder knowingly allowed defendant to use the card.

prosecution_strengths: Financial records tracing the movement and layering of funds through multiple accounts.
Cash transaction reports and Suspicious Activity Reports filed by financial institutions.
Expert testimony explaining complex financial transactions and laundering techniques.
defense_opportunities: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the funds were proceeds of unlawful activity.
Legitimate business transactions — funds were from lawful sources and the transactions had legitimate purposes.
Challenge the predicate offense — money laundering requires proof that funds came from specified unlawful activity.
Fourth Amendment challenges to financial record seizures and subpoenas.
common_defenses: No knowledge of illegal source — defendant did not know and had no reason to know the funds were from illegal activity.
Legitimate business purpose — the financial transactions had a lawful business justification.
No predicate offense — prosecution cannot prove the funds were proceeds of specified unlawful activity.
Insufficient evidence — the financial trail does not conclusively link defendant to the laundering scheme.

prosecution_strengths: Documentary evidence of false representations — contracts, emails, advertisements, and statements.
Victim testimony about reliance on defendant's misrepresentations.
Financial records showing defendant obtained money or property through the fraudulent scheme.
Pattern evidence showing multiple victims or repeated fraudulent conduct.
defense_opportunities: Good faith belief — defendant genuinely believed the representations were true.
No material misrepresentation — the alleged false statement was not material or did not cause reliance.
Puffery vs. fraud — statements were opinions, projections, or sales puffery, not actionable fraud.
Victim's failure to exercise due diligence — victim could have verified the claims but chose not to.
common_defenses: Good faith — defendant honestly believed in the truth of the representations made.
No intent to defraud — defendant did not intend to deceive or obtain property through false pretenses.
No material false statement — the alleged misrepresentation was not material or was a matter of opinion.
Lack of reliance — the victim did not actually rely on the defendant's statements in making their decision.

prosecution_strengths: Documented misrepresentations in offering documents, prospectuses, and communications.
Financial records showing investor losses tied to the fraudulent scheme.
Expert testimony on securities regulations and standard disclosures.
defense_opportunities: No material misrepresentation — disclosures were adequate and accurate.
Reliance on counsel — defendant relied on legal and financial advisors for compliance.
Good faith belief in the investment's legitimacy.
Market forces, not fraud, caused the investor losses.
common_defenses: No material misrepresentation — all material facts were disclosed to investors.
Good faith — defendant genuinely believed in the legitimacy of the investment opportunity.
Reliance on professionals — defendant relied on attorneys, accountants, and advisors for compliance.
Market loss, not fraud — investor losses resulted from market conditions, not misrepresentations.

prosecution_strengths: Forensic evidence including DNA, rape kit analysis, and physical evidence of assault.
Victim testimony, while emotionally difficult, carries significant weight with Florida juries.
defense_opportunities: Consent defense — the sexual contact was consensual between the parties.
Challenge forensic evidence — DNA shows contact but does not prove non-consent.
False accusation — motive for fabrication (custody dispute, revenge, financial gain).
Alibi — defendant was not present at the time and place of the alleged assault.
common_defenses: Consent — the sexual activity was consensual between the parties.
False accusation — the allegation is fabricated, with evidence of motive (custody dispute, anger, financial gain).
Mistaken identity — DNA evidence is absent or inconclusive, and identification is based on unreliable factors.
Insufficient evidence — prosecution cannot prove non-consent beyond reasonable doubt.

prosecution_strengths: DNA evidence from rape kit provides forensic identification.
Victim testimony about force, coercion, or incapacitation.
Medical examination documenting physical injuries consistent with sexual assault.
defense_opportunities: Consent defense where applicable — the sexual activity was consensual.
Challenge DNA evidence — presence of DNA does not establish non-consent.
Challenge victim's credibility — inconsistencies in statements, motive to fabricate.
Alibi defense — defendant was not present at the time and location.
common_defenses: Consent — the sexual activity was consensual between the parties.
Misidentification — defendant is not the perpetrator; DNA or identification evidence is inconclusive.
False accusation — victim has a motive to fabricate the allegation.
Insufficient physical evidence — no forensic evidence corroborates the allegation.

prosecution_strengths: Witness testimony about the exposure in a public or semi-public place.
