Surveillance footage capturing the indecent exposure.
Repeat offenses become felonies with potential sex offender registration.
defense_opportunities: No lewd intent — exposure was accidental (wardrobe malfunction, changing clothes, medical necessity).
Location was not public — exposure occurred in a private setting without intent for others to observe.
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who exposed themselves.
Challenge whether the conduct was lewd or lascivious rather than merely incidental.
common_defenses: Accidental exposure — the exposure was unintentional (wardrobe malfunction, urination necessity).
No lewd intent — defendant did not intend the exposure to be lewd or lascivious.
Private location — the exposure occurred in a location with a reasonable expectation of privacy.
Misidentification — defendant was not the person observed exposing themselves.

prosecution_strengths: Undercover operations with recorded audio/video of the solicitation.
Text messages, online communications, and financial transactions documenting the solicitation.
Second offense is a 1st degree misdemeanor; third or subsequent is a 3rd degree felony.
defense_opportunities: Entrapment — law enforcement initiated and induced the solicitation.
No agreement — mere discussion or inquiry does not constitute solicitation without an agreement to exchange sex for money.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who made the solicitation.
Protected speech — online discussions or advertisements may be protected First Amendment activity.
common_defenses: Entrapment — law enforcement agents initiated and persistently encouraged the defendant to solicit.
No agreement to exchange — conversation did not include an explicit agreement for sexual acts in exchange for money.
Mistaken identity — defendant was not the person who communicated with the undercover officer.
First offense diversion — many Florida counties offer diversion programs for first-time solicitation charges.

prosecution_strengths: Victim testimony about the unwanted sexual contact is often the primary evidence.
Forensic evidence (DNA, trace evidence) corroborating the contact.
Medical documentation of injuries or physical evidence of contact.
defense_opportunities: Consent — the contact was consensual between adults.
False accusation — motive to fabricate (relationship conflict, custody, revenge).
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who committed the contact offense.
Contact was incidental or accidental, not sexual in nature.
common_defenses: Consent — the sexual contact was consensual between the parties.
False accusation — the allegation is fabricated with a demonstrable motive.
Accidental contact — the touching was incidental and not sexual in nature or intent.
Insufficient evidence — prosecution cannot prove non-consent or sexual intent beyond reasonable doubt.

prosecution_strengths: Digital forensic evidence from devices, cloud accounts, and internet history.
IP address tracing and device identification linking defendant to the digital offense.
Screenshots, downloads, and chat logs documenting the offense.
Law enforcement tools for recovering deleted digital evidence.
defense_opportunities: Device was shared, hacked, or used by someone else — defendant did not commit the digital offense.
Unknowing possession — files were downloaded automatically (malware, pop-ups) without defendant's knowledge.
Age verification — defendant reasonably believed the person in communications was an adult.
Challenge digital forensic methodology — data integrity, chain of custody, and expert qualifications.
common_defenses: Unauthorized device access — someone else used defendant's device, account, or network.
No knowledge — defendant did not knowingly possess, access, or transmit the digital material.
Reasonable belief of adult age — defendant believed the other person was an adult based on representations.
Digital forensic flaws — challenge the integrity of evidence recovery, chain of custody, or expert methodology.

prosecution_strengths: Digital forensic evidence on defendant's devices including hash-matched known CSAM files.
Internet activity logs and download records documenting access to illegal material.
Federal prosecution threat with mandatory minimum of 5 years for distribution.
defense_opportunities: Unauthorized access — malware, hacking, or third-party use of defendant's device or network.
No knowledge — defendant did not know the content was present or what it contained.
Challenge digital forensic methodology — automated scanning, hash matching, and data recovery reliability.
Age of depicted person — prosecution must prove the subject is under 18.
common_defenses: Unauthorized access — defendant's computer or account was compromised by malware or third-party access.
No knowledge of content — files were downloaded unknowingly through automatic processes or pop-ups.
Digital forensic challenge — hash matching errors, unreliable forensic tools, or contaminated evidence.
Not a minor — prosecution cannot prove the depicted person is under 18 years of age.

prosecution_strengths: FDLE registry records document registration requirements and compliance deadlines.
Law enforcement verification checks document non-compliance.
Knowledge of registration requirement is presumed from prior registration or court order.
defense_opportunities: Challenge knowledge of the requirement — defendant was not informed or notification was inadequate.
Substantial compliance — defendant attempted to register but was prevented by circumstances.
Challenge the underlying conviction requiring registration — if overturned, registration requirement is void.
Homelessness or transience — argue the requirement is impossible to comply with given defendant's circumstances.
common_defenses: Lack of actual knowledge — defendant was not properly notified of the registration requirement or changes to it.
Substantial compliance — defendant made good-faith efforts to register but encountered obstacles.
Invalid predicate — the underlying conviction requiring registration has been overturned, vacated, or no longer qualifies.
Impossibility — defendant was homeless, transient, or otherwise unable to comply due to circumstances beyond their control.

prosecution_strengths: Age is established through birth certificates, school records, and testimony.
Florida has limited Romeo and Juliet provisions — only applies to 16-17 year olds with close-in-age partners.
No consent defense — victim's consent is legally irrelevant when below the age of consent.
defense_opportunities: Reasonable mistake of age — in limited circumstances, defendant's reasonable belief about the victim's age.
Challenge the evidence of sexual activity — prosecution must prove sexual contact occurred.
Constitutional challenges to age-of-consent laws as applied to specific circumstances.
common_defenses: Reasonable mistake of age — defendant reasonably believed the other person was of legal age based on appearance and representations.
Close-in-age/Romeo and Juliet — defendant and alleged victim are close in age, qualifying for exemption or mitigation.
No sexual activity — prosecution cannot prove that sexual contact actually occurred.
Constitutional challenge — application of the statute to the specific facts raises due process or equal protection concerns.

prosecution_strengths: DNA and forensic evidence from sexual assault examination kits.
Victim testimony about the force, coercion, or incapacitation used.
defense_opportunities: Consent — the sexual activity was consensual between the parties.
Challenge forensic evidence — DNA confirms contact but does not prove non-consent.
False accusation — demonstrated motive for fabrication.
Alibi — defendant was not at the location at the relevant time.
common_defenses: Consent — the sexual activity was consensual between adults.
False accusation — the allegation is fabricated, supported by evidence of motive (custody, revenge, financial).
Misidentification — forensic evidence does not conclusively identify the defendant.
Insufficient evidence of force or coercion — prosecution cannot prove beyond reasonable doubt that the activity was non-consensual.

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony about the disruptive behavior and public disturbance.
Bodycam footage showing defendant's conduct and refusal to comply.
Witness testimony corroborating the disturbance.
defense_opportunities: First Amendment — much disorderly conduct involves protected speech or expression.
Overbreadth challenge — Florida's disorderly conduct statute has been narrowed by courts.
Conduct was not public — occurred in a private setting.
De minimis conduct — the behavior was not serious enough to constitute a breach of peace.
common_defenses: Protected speech — defendant's conduct was constitutionally protected expression under the First Amendment.
No breach of peace — the conduct did not actually disturb the public peace or create a clear and present danger.
Private location — the conduct occurred in a private setting, not in a public place.
Vagueness/overbreadth — the statute's application to defendant's conduct is unconstitutionally vague.

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony about defendant's refusal to comply, fleeing, or physical resistance.
Bodycam footage documenting the resistance and officers' commands.
Injuries to officers during the arrest strengthen the with-violence charge.
defense_opportunities: Unlawful arrest — resisting an unlawful arrest is a defense in Florida (but limited).
Challenge the officer's account — bodycam footage may contradict the officer's testimony.
Passive noncompliance vs. active resistance — freezing, going limp, or verbal objection may not constitute resistance.
Excessive force — defendant's reaction was in response to the officer's unlawful use of excessive force.
common_defenses: Unlawful arrest — the underlying arrest was not supported by probable cause, making resistance to it defensible.
No obstruction — defendant's conduct did not actually obstruct the officer in performing their lawful duties.
Excessive force response — defendant reacted to the officer's use of excessive or unlawful force.
Passive noncompliance — defendant's failure to immediately comply was not active resistance or obstruction.

prosecution_strengths: Giving false information to police during investigation.
Witness tampering, evidence destruction, or harboring a fugitive.
Officer testimony about defendant's specific obstructive conduct.
defense_opportunities: Fifth Amendment right to remain silent — silence cannot constitute obstruction.
Defendant's conduct did not actually obstruct the officer's lawful execution of duty.
First Amendment — verbal criticism of police is protected speech, not obstruction.
Officer was not engaged in lawful execution of duty at the time.
common_defenses: No obstruction — defendant's conduct did not actually hinder or obstruct the officer's lawful duties.
Exercise of constitutional rights — defendant was exercising their right to remain silent, refuse consent, or speak freely.
Officer not in lawful execution — the officer was not performing a lawful duty at the time of the alleged obstruction.
Lack of willfulness — defendant's conduct was not intentional obstruction.

prosecution_strengths: Court records document the specific order that was violated.
Judge's own observations of courtroom conduct for direct contempt.
Documentary evidence of non-compliance with court orders (failure to pay, failure to appear).
Florida distinguishes direct contempt (in court) from indirect contempt (outside court).
defense_opportunities: Inability to comply — defendant was financially or physically unable to comply with the court order.
Ambiguous order — the court order was unclear about what was required.
Purge provision — for civil contempt, defendant can comply to purge the contempt finding.
Due process — indirect contempt requires notice and an opportunity to be heard.
common_defenses: Inability to comply — defendant made good faith efforts but was unable to comply due to circumstances beyond their control.
Ambiguous order — the court order was unclear, and defendant's interpretation was reasonable.
Substantial compliance — defendant substantially complied with the court order.
Due process violation — defendant was not given adequate notice and opportunity to be heard before being held in contempt.

prosecution_strengths: When charged, officer testimony about behavior, appearance, and danger to self or others.
Breathalyzer or blood test results confirming intoxication level.
defense_opportunities: Marchman Act protective custody is the proper alternative — not criminal prosecution.
Defendant was not in a public place or was not endangering others.
Medical condition mimicking intoxication (diabetes, medication effects, neurological condition).
common_defenses: Not in public — defendant was on private property or in a location not considered public.
Medical condition — defendant's behavior was caused by a medical condition, not intoxication.
Marchman Act alternative — defendant should have been taken into protective custody, not charged criminally.

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony about defendant's presence and conduct in the specific location.
Trespass warnings or prior orders to leave from the property establish notice.
Surveillance footage or repeated police contacts documenting the pattern.
defense_opportunities: Right to be present — defendant was in a public place with a right to be there.
No safety concern — defendant's presence did not create a reasonable concern for safety of persons or property.
First Amendment — defendant was engaged in protected activity (panhandling, leafleting, protesting).
common_defenses: Vagueness — the loitering statute is unconstitutionally vague as applied to defendant's conduct.
Right to be present — defendant had a lawful right to be in the public space.
No safety threat — defendant's presence did not pose a concern for the safety of persons or property.
Protected activity — defendant was engaged in constitutionally protected activity.

prosecution_strengths: Witness testimony about the noise, disturbance, or disruptive behavior.
Audio or video recordings capturing the disturbance.
Multiple complaints from different sources corroborating the disruption.
Florida's breach of peace provisions cover a range of disruptive public conduct.
defense_opportunities: First Amendment — noise and speech in public spaces may be constitutionally protected.
Reasonable conduct — defendant's behavior was not objectively disturbing to a reasonable person.
Private property — disturbance occurred on private property with limited public impact.
Selective enforcement — defendant was singled out while others engaged in similar conduct.
common_defenses: Protected expression — defendant's conduct involved constitutionally protected speech or assembly.
Not a disturbance — the conduct did not actually disturb the peace or breach public order.
Private location — the conduct occurred in a private setting with limited public impact.
Selective enforcement — similarly situated individuals were not charged.

prosecution_strengths: Court records document the hearing date, notice to defendant, and defendant's absence.
Bail bond documents showing defendant's obligation to appear.
FTA triggers bench warrant and potential bail revocation.
defense_opportunities: Lack of notice — defendant did not receive actual notice of the hearing date.
Excusable absence — medical emergency, incarceration in another jurisdiction, or other compelling reason.
Prompt voluntary appearance — defendant appeared as soon as possible after the missed date.
Challenge whether the underlying proceeding was properly noticed.
common_defenses: Lack of notice — defendant was not properly notified of the court date and did not know about the hearing.
Good cause — defendant was unable to appear due to medical emergency, hospitalization, or incarceration elsewhere.
Voluntary surrender — defendant voluntarily appeared shortly after the missed date, demonstrating no intent to evade.
Administrative error — court records contain errors about the hearing date or notice.

prosecution_strengths: Documentation of the false report in police records.
Investigation records showing the report was knowingly false.
Witness testimony or physical evidence contradicting the false report.
defense_opportunities: Good faith belief — defendant genuinely believed the report was true when made.
Mistake of fact — defendant was mistaken about the circumstances but did not knowingly lie.
Coercion — defendant was coerced or pressured into making the false report.
Recantation — defendant corrected the false report before it caused significant harm.
common_defenses: Good faith — defendant genuinely believed the information reported was true.
Mistake of fact — defendant was honestly mistaken about what occurred.
No knowledge of falsity — defendant did not know the report was false at the time it was made.
Coercion — defendant was pressured or threatened into making the false report.

prosecution_strengths: Written threats (texts, emails, social media) provide documentary evidence of the threat.
Victim testimony about receiving the threat and resulting fear.
Context evidence showing the defendant's motive and intent behind the threat.
defense_opportunities: Conditional or hyperbolic statement — the statement was not a genuine threat of imminent harm.
No intent — defendant did not intend the statement as a threat; it was venting, humor, or protected speech.
Context — the statement was made in a context (online argument, song lyrics, fiction) that negates threat interpretation.
common_defenses: Not a true threat — the statement was hyperbolic, conditional, or not intended as a genuine threat of harm.
Protected speech — the statement is protected expression under the First Amendment.
No intent to threaten — defendant did not intend the communication as a threat.
Context — the statement was made in a context (fiction, art, online argument) that negates its threatening nature.

prosecution_strengths: Pattern of unwanted communications documented through phone records, texts, and social media.
Victim testimony about the course of conduct causing substantial emotional distress.
Injunction/restraining order violations can elevate the charge.
defense_opportunities: Legitimate purpose — communications were for a lawful purpose (debt collection, shared custody, business).
No course of conduct — isolated incidents do not constitute harassment.
First Amendment — speech directed at a public matter is protected.
Mutual communications — both parties were engaging in the communications voluntarily.
common_defenses: Legitimate purpose — the communications served a lawful purpose (business, shared children, legal matter).
No course of conduct — the behavior was isolated, not a repeated pattern of harassment.
Protected expression — the communications involve constitutionally protected speech.
No substantial emotional distress — the victim was not actually placed in substantial distress by the conduct.

prosecution_strengths: Probation officer testimony about specific conditions violated.
Lower burden of proof — preponderance of evidence, not beyond reasonable doubt.
Documentary evidence of non-compliance (failed drug tests, missed appointments, new arrests).
Court has broad discretion in sentencing upon revocation, including the maximum original sentence.
defense_opportunities: Substantial compliance — defendant complied with most conditions and the violation is minor.
Circumstances beyond defendant's control prevented compliance (job loss, illness, transportation).
Technical violation vs. new law violation — courts may distinguish between the severity of violations.
Modify conditions rather than revoke — argue for continued probation with modified terms.
common_defenses: Substantial compliance — defendant complied with the majority of probation conditions.
Inability to comply — circumstances beyond defendant's control prevented compliance (financial hardship, medical emergency).
Modification over revocation — argue that modified probation conditions are more appropriate than incarceration.
Due process — defendant was not given adequate notice of the alleged violation or opportunity to respond.

prosecution_strengths: Probation records documenting missed check-ins, failed drug tests, or travel without permission.
Probation officer testimony about the technical violations.
Lower burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence standard.
Cumulative effect of multiple technical violations shows pattern of non-compliance.
defense_opportunities: De minimis violation — minor technical violations may not warrant revocation.
Good cause for non-compliance — employment conflict, medical issue, or communication breakdown.
Graduated sanctions — argue for intermediate sanctions rather than revocation.
Completion of most probation requirements demonstrates overall compliance.
common_defenses: Good cause — defendant had a legitimate reason for the technical non-compliance.
De minimis — the violation was minor and does not warrant revocation of probation.
Alternative sanctions — request graduated sanctions (additional community service, increased reporting) rather than revocation.
Substantial compliance — defendant has otherwise been compliant with all major probation conditions.

prosecution_strengths: New criminal charge provides direct evidence of the substantive violation.
Police reports and arrest records for the new offense.
Preponderance of evidence standard — lower than the reasonable doubt required for the new charge itself.
Court may revoke even if the new charge is ultimately dismissed or results in acquittal.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the evidence of the new offense — if the new charge is weak, the violation may be contestable.
Acquittal or dismissal of the new charge, while not binding, is persuasive.
Self-defense or other justification for the new alleged offense.
Negotiate resolution — concurrent disposition of the violation and new charge.
common_defenses: Insufficient evidence of new offense — even under preponderance standard, the evidence does not support the allegation.
Justification — defendant had a legal justification (self-defense) for the conduct underlying the new charge.
Dismissal of new charge — while not dispositive, dismissal of the underlying charge is strongly persuasive.
Mitigating circumstances — argue for modified probation rather than revocation based on the circumstances.

prosecution_strengths: Community control (Florida's house arrest) has strict conditions — GPS monitoring provides objective violation evidence.
Community control officer's testimony about detected violations is detailed and contemporaneous.
GPS data, curfew violations, and zone violations are electronically documented.
Court may impose up to the maximum original sentence upon revocation.
defense_opportunities: GPS equipment malfunction — electronic monitoring devices have known accuracy issues.
Emergency circumstance — defendant left the approved area due to medical emergency or safety threat.
Ambiguous zone boundaries — GPS zones may not perfectly correspond to approved locations.
Good faith compliance effort — argue defendant substantially complied and the violation was inadvertent.
common_defenses: Equipment malfunction — GPS monitoring equipment malfunctioned, creating a false violation alert.
Emergency — defendant left the approved area due to a genuine emergency (medical, safety).
Substantial compliance — defendant has otherwise been fully compliant with community control conditions.
Ambiguous conditions — the terms of community control were unclear about the specific restriction violated.

prosecution_strengths: Florida Commission on Offender Review sets parole conditions and monitors compliance.
Parole officer testimony about specific violations and defendant's compliance history.
Lower burden of proof — preponderance of evidence.
Revocation can result in return to prison for the remainder of the original sentence.
defense_opportunities: Substantial compliance with parole conditions overall.
Circumstances beyond defendant's control prevented compliance.
Violation was minor or technical, not warranting full revocation.
Positive factors since parole — employment, family stability, community involvement.
common_defenses: Substantial compliance — defendant has generally complied with parole conditions and the violation is isolated.
Good cause — circumstances beyond defendant's control prevented compliance with the specific condition.
Modification over revocation — request modified parole conditions rather than return to prison.
Due process — inadequate notice of the violation or opportunity to be heard.

prosecution_strengths: Supervising officer documentation of the violation.
Similar to probation/parole violations — lower evidentiary standard.
Court records of the release conditions and documented non-compliance.
Any new arrest during supervised release is a serious violation.
defense_opportunities: Argue the violation is technical and does not warrant modification or revocation.
Good cause for non-compliance — employment, medical, or family circumstances.
Positive adjustment since release — employment, treatment completion, community ties.
Graduated sanctions rather than revocation.
common_defenses: Good cause — defendant had a legitimate reason for the technical non-compliance.
Substantial compliance — defendant has otherwise been compliant with release conditions.
Alternative disposition — graduated sanctions or modified conditions rather than revocation.
Positive post-release adjustment — defendant has demonstrated rehabilitation through employment and community ties.

prosecution_strengths: Co-conspirator statements admissible under hearsay exception during the course and in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Cooperating co-defendant testimony about the agreement and plan.
Electronic communications (texts, calls, emails) documenting the conspiratorial agreement.
defense_opportunities: No agreement — defendant did not agree to commit the offense with another person.
Withdrawal — defendant withdrew from the conspiracy before the overt act and communicated withdrawal to co-conspirators.
Mere presence or association — being present or knowing about a plan is not conspiracy.
common_defenses: No agreement — defendant did not enter into an agreement to commit the underlying offense.
Withdrawal — defendant withdrew from the conspiracy and communicated that withdrawal to co-conspirators before any overt act.
Mere association — defendant's relationship with co-conspirators does not prove agreement to commit a crime.
Entrapment — government agents created the conspiracy and induced defendant to participate.

prosecution_strengths: Prosecution must disprove self-defense beyond reasonable doubt once raised — but can present evidence the force was unreasonable.
Physical evidence (injuries, scene reconstruction) may contradict the self-defense narrative.
Prior relationship between parties may show aggression pattern by the defendant.
Disproportionate force — response greatly exceeded the threat level.
defense_opportunities: Pretrial immunity hearing — if successful, charges are dismissed without trial.
Burden shifts to prosecution to disprove self-defense beyond reasonable doubt.
common_defenses: Reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm — defendant's subjective and objective fear was reasonable under the circumstances.
Defense of others — defendant used force to protect a third person from imminent unlawful force.

prosecution_strengths: Florida criminal code covers a wide range of offenses beyond the common categories.
Specific statutory language defines the elements clearly for each unique offense.
Documented evidence specific to the charged offense.
Expert testimony when the offense involves specialized knowledge.
defense_opportunities: Statutory interpretation — challenge whether defendant's conduct falls within the statute's language.
Constitutional challenge — vagueness, overbreadth, or as-applied constitutional arguments.
Element-by-element defense — identify the weakest element and attack it specifically.
Diversion or alternative disposition where available for less serious offenses.
common_defenses: Statutory construction — defendant's conduct does not fall within the plain language of the statute.
Constitutional challenge — the statute is unconstitutionally vague, overbroad, or violates due process as applied.
Insufficient evidence — prosecution cannot prove all elements beyond reasonable doubt.
Mistake of fact or law — defendant's reasonable misunderstanding of the law or facts negates the required mental state.
